newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt confirms intention to sell power stations.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt confirms intention to sell power stations.

text.p: Eight power stations the government considers are not part of the core business of state-owned generator Electricity Corporation of New Zealand will be sold, ministers said on Monday.

In a joint statement, Treasurer Winston Peters, Finance Minister Bill Birch and State-Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley said if the stations were not sold "after a defined period" they would be transferred to the smaller state-owned generator, Contact Energy.

The stations are Matahina near Whakatane, the Coleridge and Highbank stations near Christchurch, Cobb near Nelson, the Kaitawa, Tuai and Piripaua stations near Lake Waikaremoana, and the Mangahao station near Levin.
The government said it was selling six stations. It treats the three Waikaremoana stations as a single unit, a spokesman for Peters said.

"These stations are available for purchase by local energy companies or Maori interests, particularly in conjunction with Treaty of Waitangi settlements. These stations are not available for sale on the open market," the ministers said.
They said the National-New Zealand First coalition government did not intend to privatise the core assets of ECNZ or Contact Energy.

Earlier Shipley and Conservation Minister Nick Smith said the stations were for sale, but Peters said before commenting he wanted to consult party negotiators who had handled that area of the coalition talks late last year, a spokesman said.

New Zealand First campaigned on a strong platform of opposing state asset sales. But with seven of its 17 MPs of Maori descent, it was seen as likely to support the sale of the small hydro-stations, some of which are included in Treaty of
Waitangi claims agreements with Maori interests, while others are being eyed by Maori for future claims.
New Zealand First and the conservative National Party formed a coalition after a gneeral election in October 1996.
The former National government first announced its intention to sell the eight stations, which together make up nearly four percent of New Zealand's generation capacity, in mid-1995.
